vignette:
Patient: Mr. Chan (pseudonym), a 69-year-old widower of Chinese-Vietnamese descent.

Mr. Chan is a small, neat man who arrives for his sessions precisely on time, often with a slight bow and a quiet apology for the weather or the traffic, as if he is responsible for any minor inconvenience. He is a nanny for a family with a two-year-old boy, a position he has held for the last four years. He speaks of this work with a gentle, practiced patience. The child, he says, is his "sunshine," a word that catches in his throat. It is this job, and the child in his care, that has finally driven him to seek help.

The story he tells begins not with the trauma, but with a memory of joy. For fifteen years, he and his wife, Linh, owned a small pho restaurant. Their only son, Minh, was their universe. Mr. Chan describes Minh’s childhood in vivid, sensory detail: the smell of star anise and cinnamon on his clothes, the sound of Minh’s laughter as he helped fold napkins, the sight of his small hand gripping a wooden spoon too big for it. This is the world that was shattered.

When Minh was nine, he began to bruise easily and grew tired. The diagnosis was acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Mr. Chan’s narrative changes here. The sentences become shorter, fragmented. He describes the hospital as a place of fluorescent lights that never dimmed and a smell of antiseptic that he can still summon in his nose. He and Linh took shifts. He would hold Minh’s hand during the spinal taps, feeling the boy’s small body go rigid with pain, and he would sing the lullabies his own mother had sung to him in Vietnam. He believed, with a desperate, unshakeable faith, that his love, his presence, his sheer will, could keep his son alive.

Minh went into remission, but the cancer returned two years later, more aggressive. Mr. Chan describes the second round of treatment as a slow, grinding erosion of hope. He watched his son, once so vibrant, become a fragile ghost. He remembers the exact moment the doctor came into the waiting room, the way the man’s shoes squeaked on the linoleum floor. He remembers the words, "I'm so sorry. We did everything we could." Minh was eleven.

The world after that, Mr. Chan says, was a silent film. He and Linh grieved in different rooms of their house. The restaurant closed. They sold their home. The marriage, he says, died of a broken heart long before Linh’s body followed, five years later. He worked odd jobs, never staying long. He felt invisible, and he preferred it that way.

Now, he is a nanny. He chose this work, he says, because he is good with children. But the truth, he admits in a whisper, is more complicated. He is trying to save a child again.

The trouble began three months ago. The two-year-old in his care, Leo, developed a persistent fever. Mr. Chan’s heart began to pound. He found himself checking Leo’s skin for bruises a dozen times a day. He would wake in the night, drenched in sweat, certain he could hear the beep of a heart monitor. He began to smell the antiseptic again, even in the clean, citrus-scented home of his employers. He started to feel a pressure in his chest, a tightness that makes him feel like he is suffocating. He is irritable with the parents, snapping at them for small things, like leaving a toy on the floor. He avoids the pediatrician’s office, his hands shaking so badly he cannot hold the car keys. He has stopped taking Leo to the park, terrified that a fall, a scrape, a simple cough, will be the beginning of the end.

He knows, intellectually, that Leo is healthy. He has the lab results. The doctor has told him. But his body does not believe it. He lives in a state of constant, low-grade terror, waiting for the other shoe to drop. He sees Minh’s face in Leo’s. He hears Minh’s laughter in Leo’s babbling. And he feels a profound, crushing guilt. He is failing this child, not by neglect, but by the sheer weight of his own fear. He is trying to protect Leo from a ghost, and in doing so, he is losing the very thing he sought to regain: the simple, joyful act of caring for a child.
